engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Strategy: Weak Squares
chess.body: A weak square is one that cannot be defended by a pawn. d5 is weak for Black if the c6 and e6 pawns are gone or never played. Plant a knight on a weak square — it becomes an 'outpost.' From d5, a knight controls 8 squares and cannot be chased. Outpost knight + weak squares = long-term advantage.

wisdom.title: On Anger
wisdom.body: Anger is information, not instruction. It tells you a boundary was crossed or a value was violated. But acting on anger rarely solves the problem. Practice: when you feel it rising, say 'I need 5 minutes' and leave the room. Return calm. Then address the issue. You can be firm without being explosive.

book.author: Phil Knight
book.lesson: Phil Knight's memoir of building Nike is a masterclass in starting before you're ready. He started by importing Japanese running shoes from Onitsuka Tiger with no retail experience, no capital, no strategy. He sold them from the boot of his car at track meets. He kept the company alive for 12 years on the edge of bankruptcy, constantly one rejected bank loan away from collapse. His key lesson: don't wait until you have it figured out. Start with the version you can afford. Learn on real customers with real money at stake. Iterate from there. Nike's swoosh was designed by a student for $35.
book.key_quote: The perfect plan never survives first contact with reality. Start imperfectly and iterate.
book.action: Identify one project you've been waiting to start until conditions are better. What is the smallest possible version you could execute this week?
crux: Knight started by importing Onitsuka Tigers from a car boot, with no capital and no plan.
Nike ran nearly insolvent for almost two decades while growing fast. Growth consumes cash.
The Crazy Idea only has to be believed by you at the start.
Bank relationships nearly killed the company more often than competitors did.
The Onitsuka betrayal forced Nike into becoming a brand rather than a distributor.
Hire obsessives and misfits. The Buttfaces argued viciously and shipped.
Bowerman's tinkering — waffle iron to waffle sole — was product development without a process.
The $8,000 the US government demanded could have ended it. Legal risk is existential risk.
Don't tell people how to do their jobs. Tell them what to do and let them surprise you.
Losing hurts more than winning feels good, and that asymmetry is fuel and poison.
Cash flow, not profit, decides whether you survive the year.
Faith outlasts evidence for a long time before evidence arrives.
Business is war without bullets — and the price is paid in family time.
learnings: Fast growth and near-bankruptcy routinely coexist. Watch cash, not revenue.
Dependence on a single supplier or channel is an existential risk, not an inconvenience.
Obsessive, difficult people build the things that matter.
The cost of building is paid by the people at home too. Count it honestly.
examples: Nike hit $8m in sales while unable to make payroll — the classic growth-cash trap.
The waffle sole came from Bowerman pouring rubber into his wife's waffle iron. No R&D budget.
Knight sold shoes out of his car at track meets for years before any retail presence.
adapt: Single-channel risk is real: Meta restriction and Railway's shutdown are the same lesson twice.
Cash first. The SIP and 6-month buffer are what let you take a career risk at all.
Ship the imperfect version. Nike's first shoes fell apart and they iterated in public.
Count the family cost of the Dubai push explicitly, and decide it's worth it — don't let it accumulate silently.

minimalism.title: The 90/90 Rule
minimalism.body: Have you used it in the last 90 days? Will you in the next 90? If both answers are no, it is storage, not ownership. You are paying rent on it in square feet and attention.

interview_tech.q: What is open-to-buy and why should finance care?
interview_tech.a: Open-to-buy is the budget available to purchase stock for a future period, given planned sales, planned markdowns and target closing stock. It is where merchandise planning and finance meet. Finance should care because it is the single control that prevents over-buying — the root cause of the markdown spiral that destroys gross margin two seasons later. If buyers can commit outside OTB without sign-off, your inventory forecast is decoration.

interview_tech.q: What is the effect of a sale-and-leaseback on your financials?
interview_tech.a: Cash in now, occupancy cost forever. You derecognise the asset, recognise a gain or loss limited to the rights transferred, and recognise a right-of-use asset and lease liability under IFRS 16 — so leverage does not fall by the full cash proceeds. It flatters current-year cash and often current-year profit while committing you to rent for 15–20 years. Legitimate for releasing capital from non-core property; a warning sign when used to plug an operating cash shortfall.

interview_soft.q: How do you handle a request from the CEO that you believe is unethical?
interview_soft.a: Slow it down without escalating to confrontation. First assume miscommunication and restate what you understood — a surprising share of these resolve there. If it holds, state your objection privately, in writing, with the specific standard or law engaged. Offer the compliant alternative that gets closest to the commercial aim. If pressed, escalate to the audit committee chair. Say plainly that you would resign rather than sign something you believe is false — the willingness is the answer they are testing for.

interview_soft.q: A peer takes credit for your team's work in front of the CEO. What do you do?
interview_soft.a: Not in the room. Afterwards, directly and without an audience: describe what you observed, not their motive, and say what you need going forward. If it repeats, correct it factually in the moment — 'just to add, the modelling on that was Priya's team' — which is a contribution rather than an accusation. Escalating first, or absorbing it silently and resenting it, are both worse. They are testing composure and whether you protect your team.

cfo_field.q: Know your break-even by store, not by chain.
cfo_field.a: A chain at group-level profitability can be carrying a quarter of its estate below contribution. Compute store contribution — gross profit less rent, staff and directly attributable fixed cost — and rank it. Then, before closing anything: is the lease committed, what does the store contribute to online fulfilment in its catchment, and what is the exit cost. A negative-contribution store with four years left on a non-cancellable lease is usually cheaper to run than to close.
cfo_field.who: The analysis that gets you noticed

cfo_field.q: VAT in the GCC is a cash-flow instrument, not just a compliance task.
cfo_field.a: Registration thresholds, filing frequency and the timing of input recovery all move working capital. A group filing quarterly rather than monthly holds recoverable input VAT longer than it needs to. Know the filing calendar in every jurisdiction the group trades in, and know which entity holds the recoverable balance — a refund stuck in the wrong entity is cash you own and cannot use.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early king safety: after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6, avoid passive moves like …Be7; develop knights, castle before 10th move, and prevent queen‑side attacks that led to mate at move 37.

lichess_summary.session_summary: Your opening choices are a disaster—every game you play collapses before the middlegame, and you haven’t even managed a single win. Stop relying on rote theory and force yourself to understand the key ideas behind the first 10 moves; pick one solid, low‑theory opening (e.g., the London System as White or the Caro‑Kann as Black) and master its pawn structures and typical plans. Immediately start a daily 30‑minute “opening drill” where you play the first 12 moves against a computer, annotate every mistake, and only then move on to the rest of the board.
